docs.title: Setup
docs.text: Install the package, then run it from a script, a REPL or a notebook.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
Install uv, which manages Python and the packages for you.

curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh

Clone the repository and install the package and its dependencies into .venv/.

git clone https://github.com/seabbs/bdbv-hub-modelling.git
cd bdbv-hub-modelling
uv sync

Run every command below from the bdbv-hub-modelling folder. The hub data are not committed. task nowcastbdbv:data (or uv run bdbvhub data) fetches the latest hub data into data/, and task nowcastbdbv:data-bvd caches the BVDOutbreakSize releases that renewalbvd reads. The tests read a frozen copy in tests/fixtures/data/, so they need no download.

docs.title: Work interactively
docs.text:
uv run runs a command inside the project's environment.

To Run Open a Python REPL uv run python Open an IPython REPL uv run --with ipython ipython Open Jupyter Lab uv run --with jupyterlab jupyter lab Run a script uv run python my_forecast.py

In VS Code, open the folder and pick .venv/bin/python as the interpreter or notebook kernel. VS Code offers to install ipykernel the first time you run a notebook cell.

docs.title: Run a forecast from a script
docs.text:
Save this as my_forecast.py in the bdbv-hub-modelling folder. It forecasts with the random walk nowcast from one release, scores the forecast against later releases and saves a table and a figure. Getting started walks through the same steps, and the API reference documents each function.

import dataclasses
from pathlib import Path

from nowcastbdbv.backtest import make_tasks
from nowcastbdbv.data.tidy import (
    delays_for_vintage,
    load_daily,
    load_delays,
    load_target,
)
from nowcasteval import backtest as bt
from nowcasteval.nowcast import relative_crps, release_backtest
from nowcastutils.base import NATIONAL
from nowcastbaselines.baselinenowcast.delays import Settings
from nowcastbaselines.randomwalk import RandomWalk, RandomWalkNowcast
from nowcasteval.plots import plot_location_grid

# Settings to change.
ORIGIN = "2026-10-17"  # the release to forecast from
N_SAMPLES = 200  # sample trajectories per location
WALK_WEEKS = 6  # weeks of data that set the random walk's spread
OUT = Path("output/my-forecast")

target, daily, delays = load_target(), load_daily(), load_delays()
real = target.loc[target["kind"] == "real"]

config = dataclasses.replace(
    bt.load_config("packages/nowcastbdbv/config/backtest.toml"), min_horizon=-6, n_samples=N_SAMPLES
)
task = make_tasks(
    real.loc[real["vintage"] == ORIGIN],
    delays_for_vintage(delays, ORIGIN)[0],
    config,
    history=real,
    daily=daily,
)[0]

models = [
    RandomWalk(),
    RandomWalkNowcast(settings=Settings(walk_weeks=WALK_WEEKS)),
]
forecasts = bt.run_forecasts(models, [task])
scores = release_backtest(
    [task], daily, target, models=(), stored=forecasts
).scores

OUT.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
forecasts.to_csv(OUT / "forecasts.csv", index=False)
table = relative_crps(scores.loc[scores["target"] == "reported"])
table.to_csv(OUT / "relative-crps.csv", index=False)
fig = plot_location_grid(forecasts, real, [NATIONAL, "CD-IT"])
fig.savefig(OUT / "forecast.png", dpi=150)
print(table)

Run it.

uv run python my_forecast.py

To change a setting, edit it at the top of the script and run it again. ORIGIN takes any release date in real["vintage"]. get_model("randomwalknowcast") builds the same model with its default settings, and bdbvhub.models.list_models() lists every model. The renewal models fit with a sampler and take minutes per task (see Renewal models).

docs.title: Where outputs land
docs.text:
Output Folder The script above output/my-forecast/ uv run bdbvhub backtest forecasts and scores in results/ uv run bdbvhub nowcast the hub file in output/submission/ uv run bdbvhub report the docs figures and tables in docs/figures/ and docs/generated/

output/ is not committed, so anything there is yours to delete.

docs.title: Adding a model
docs.text:
Adding a model to the registry, so every evaluation includes it.

A model is a class with a name and a forecast(task) method. task is a ForecastTask: the target rows and delay data of one vintage, the provinces and weeks to forecast, the number of samples and a seed. forecast returns one row per location, week and sample, with columns location, target_end_date, sample and value.

from dataclasses import dataclass

import pandas as pd

from nowcastutils.base import ForecastTask, register_model


@dataclass
class MyModel:
    name: str = "my_model"

    def forecast(self, task: ForecastTask) -> pd.DataFrame: ...


register_model("my_model", MyModel, "One line describing it.")

Import the module in bdbvhub/models.py. The backtest, the Backtest and Nowcast pages, compare-hub and nowcast --model my_model then include it. The backtest adds the national total, the horizons and the vintage kind.

For the leave-one-province-out check, set supports_mask = True and drop the provinces in task.mask from the likelihood while still forecasting them.

docs.title: Renewal variants
docs.text:
A new renewal variant is one entry in VARIANTS in nowcastrenewal.forecaster. It names a base ModelConfig and the fields it changes. Fitted variants are not run by the docs build or the smoke tests. The fit store fits them once a variant is on main. To fit one locally, run bdbvhub fit-store fit --model <name> --origin <date> --store output/fit-store for each origin, then bdbvhub fit-store load --store output/fit-store. task bdbvhub:backtest then scores them with the other models.

BDBV_RENEWAL_SAMPLER sets the NUTS settings of leave-one-province-out fits.

docs.title: CLI
docs.text:
The bdbvhub command.

Paths to the tidy data default to $BDBV_DATA_DIR or data/. bdbvhub <command> --help lists each command's options.

Command What it does data Download the hub data and write the tidy tables to data/. backtest Run the development backtest, the evaluation on the real releases (results/nowcast-*.csv). Fitted models are never run: their rows in results/ come from the fit store and are kept. With --models, only those models run and the others' rows are kept. backtest --lopo Leave one province out: forecast each province with its counts masked, for the variants that take a mask. bvd Cache the BVDOutbreakSize releases each vintage may use. compare-hub [--fetch] Score our retrospective forecasts and the hub's submitted ones on the same truth and weeks. nowcast Forecast from a real vintage, write the hub file and check it. With --config and --fit, forecast from a fit configuration. zone-backtest Score the zone runs of randomwalk and randomwalknowcast that the fit store holds, for the fits fit-store load used, on the real vintages. --chunk K/N scores only block K of N of the origins. fit-store plan, fit, load, unpack List the fits the fit store lacks (--origins for some origins), make one, load the stored fits into results/, or write a submission candidate's stored fit directory for the submission. fit Fit a configuration and write the fit directory and its diagnostics, for the submission CI. plot-submission Plot a submitted hub file. plot-ppc Plot a fit's posterior predictive checks (ppc.json). coherence Compare the national data with the sum of the provinces. validate Run the hub's checks on files. metadata Write and check a model's metadata YAML. hub-id Print the hub model id that submissions use. freeze-round Write a round's docs page to the ledger once its pull request has merged. report Make the docs figures and tables. digest [--with PATH...] [--text TEXT] [--model M] Print a hash of what a backtest reads, which keys its cached outputs in the Site workflow. With --model, only that model's code (its import closure, less the other models' modules) with the data. backtest --forecast-only Forecast without scoring and write the forecasts to --parts, so each model can run apart. score PART... Score the forecasts of --forecast-only runs, every model together, and write the results files one run of each backtest writes. concat-results --out DIR [--dedupe FILE...] PART... Stack the results files of runs made apart, such as blocks of dates, in the order given. --dedupe keeps one copy of rows every part writes in full.

--version prints the package version.

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text:
task bdbvhub:backtest           # development backtest and real releases
task bdbvhub:backtest-lopo      # leave one province out
task bdbvhub:backtest-zones     # random walk models at health-zone level
task bdbvhub:results            # every derived file in results/, as the Pages build makes them
task docs                            # build the site into _site/ (runs task bdbvhub:results, about 25 min)
task serve                           # serve the site (run task bdbvhub:results once first)

--models runs some models and keeps the others' rows in results/. The files in results/ are not committed. The Pages build makes the rest with the steps of task bdbvhub:results, from the code, the data and the fit store.

docs.title: Fit store
docs.text:
The backtest and the docs build fit no model. The Fit store workflow (.github/workflows/fit-store.yml) fits each fitted model once at each real origin. Each fit is one file on the fit-store branch, <model>/<origin>/<key>.json.gz. The key hashes:

  • the task at the origin, which holds only the releases up to it;
  • the model as built, including its variant and sampler settings;
  • the BVDOutbreakSize release, for renewalbvd;
  • the code the model's fit can run (its import closure with bdbvhub/store/store.py and nowcasteval/backtest.py), without docstrings or comments; the zone backtest (nowcastbdbv/zones.py) is left out, as a fit does not run it; so are the key's own helper (bdbvhub/store/digest.py) and the plots (nowcasteval/plots.py), which a fit does not run;
  • the package's data files (packages/nowcastbdbv/src/nowcastbdbv/data/*.csv), such as the province centres of the gravity kernel;
  • the runtime dependencies in uv.lock.

The renewal variants use the sampler table of the submission candidate that runs them, in packages/bdbvsubmission/policy.toml. A model code or sampler change refits every origin. A new hub release adds one fit per model. The task at each origin is the submission's (nowcastbdbv.backtest.vintage_task): weeks from 6 before the reference date to one week past [forecast] max_horizon, so the next round can be forecast from the same fit when no new release comes, and the latest earlier delays for a release with none of its own. The backtest loads the weeks from [forecast] min_horizon to max_horizon. A submission candidate's fit also holds the fit directory the submission reads (samples, ppc.json and diagnostics.json), and the submission forecasts from it (fit-store unpack).

The workflow runs on pushes to main that change these inputs, every 6 hours for new hub releases, and when the submission finds a round's fits missing. It fits and stores the newest origin first, then the other origins, so a backfill never holds up a round. A push never cancels a running refit: the latest push waits and runs after it. The fit jobs are read-only, and one job with no project code pushes their files and prunes the branch. It keeps the current key's file and the newest good fit of older code for each model and origin. A fit that fails is stored as failed, and is fitted again only when its inputs change or a dispatch sets retry_failed. On a pull request the workflow only lists the fits the change needs. Only main writes to fit-store. To test a branch, dispatch the workflow on it with store_branch set to a name starting fit-store-scratch, and models to limit it. Any other store_branch stops the run. When fits are stored, the workflow rebuilds the docs.

task bdbvhub:fit-store-plan  # the fits the store lacks for this code and data
task bdbvhub:fit-store       # load the stored fits into results/

task bdbvhub:backtest loads the store first. Where the store has no fit for the current key, load uses the newest stored fit of that model and origin. Pages with fitted-model results list the commits of their fits and the fits not yet made. A full refit is 20 fits (4 models at 5 origins): 43 minutes and 5.3 runner-hours, with the slowest fit 39 minutes (renewalbvd). A new release adds 4 fits: about 40 minutes and 1.3 runner-hours.

To fit a model locally, for example a new variant:

uv run bdbvhub fit-store fit --model renewal --origin 2026-10-24 --store output/fit-store
uv run bdbvhub fit-store load --store output/fit-store

The comparison with hub forecasts downloads other teams' files, so it is run on its own:

uv run bdbvhub compare-hub --fetch

docs.title: Hub files
docs.text:
bdbvhub nowcast writes model-output/<model_id>/<reference_date>-<model_id>.csv under output/submission/. The model id is seabbs- plus the model's model_abbr in packages/bdbvhub/config/hub.toml. When the reference date is an open round in tasks.json, it checks the file with submission.validate, the Python port of the hub's checks:

  • column names and order free, no extra columns;
  • one reference date, listed in tasks.json;
  • known locations, the one target and sample output only;
  • target weeks listed in tasks.json;
  • exactly 100 samples per location, and every sample covers the same weeks;
  • integer sample ids, finite non-negative values, no duplicate rows.

It skips the submission window and the model metadata, which bdbvhub metadata checks. For any other reference date it prints a note and skips the checks.

task bdbvhub:validate then runs the hub's own hubValidations::validate_submission() in R against a fresh clone of the hub.

bdbvhub metadata writes packages/bdbvsubmission/model-metadata/<model id>.yml and checks it against the hub's schema.

Sample ids

Sample ids run from 1 to 100 and are shared across locations, so hubValidations reads samples as joint across locations.

The bdbvhub API reference documents main and build_parser.

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text:
Setting up, checking and documenting changes to the package.

Task What it does task setup Install the package with the dev and docs groups. task test Run the tests with coverage. task test-slow Run the tests marked slow (model fits and Chronos-2 inference). task lint Lint with ruff, check formatting and type-check with mypy. task format Format and fix lint where safe. task docs Build the docs strictly into _site/. task submission:test Lint, type-check and test the submission CI scripts in packages/bdbvsubmission/.

Pre-commit hooks run the same checks on each commit. The docs build, not pytest coverage, runs the reporting code end to end. New behaviour comes with a test, and docs follow UK English with one sentence per line. The docs read generated tables, so build them with task docs, not mkdocs build. New models are added as on Adding a model.

docs.title: Fine-tuned foundation
docs.text:
We fine-tune the Chronos-2 forecasting model on simulated outbreaks so that it can nowcast from a reporting triangle laid out as series. The fine-tuned model forecasts daily and weekly series in one joint block, for the country, the provinces and the health zones. We compare it with randomwalknowcast from nowcastbaselines, our JAX port of baselinenowcast with a random walk on top, which we develop as part of the paper. This section is for readers of the paper and for anyone who wants to use the fine-tuned checkpoints on their own data.

flowchart LR
    SIM["Outbreaks simulated<br/>with a joint renewal model"] --> TRI["Reporting triangles<br/>as series"]
    TRI --> FT["Chronos-2 fine-tuned<br/>LoRA and attention biases"]
    FT --> OUT["One joint block<br/>daily and weekly<br/>country, provinces, zones"]

The outbreaks come from one PyRenew model, from latent infections to reported counts (nowcastrenewal.simulation), with each simulation's settings drawn from a grid (nowcastfoundation.simulator).

docs.title: Where to start
docs.text:
• To use a checkpoint, start with Using the fine-tuned model.
  • To reproduce the simulation, training and scoring, start with the workflow, one Snakemake target per step.

docs.title: In this section
docs.text:
• Paper: the main text and the supporting information, which hold the methods (the simulation grid, the training and the evaluation) and the results.
  • Using the fine-tuned model: loading a released checkpoint and nowcasting your own reporting triangle.
  • German nowcast benchmark: the paper's retrospective case study.

The code is in nowcastfoundation, nowcastrenewal and nowcastbaselines. How the hub submission uses these models is on Foundation models and Baseline models, under Hub submission.

Next: Paper.

docs.title: Hub submission
docs.text: Each week we submit forecasts to the BDBV Modeling Hub. We evaluate every model against the random walk and the random walk nowcast on the hub's own releases, and compare them with the other hub teams. We submit the random walk nowcast as seabbs-rwnowcast, the first renewal model to pass its checks as seabbs-renewal, and the fine-tuned foundation model as seabbs-foundation once it is opted in (Submission workflow).

docs.title: Where to start
docs.text:
• To see this week's forecasts, start with Nowcast.
  • To run a model yourself, start with the bdbvhub command (CLI): bdbvhub data, then bdbvhub nowcast.
  • To see how a round is submitted, start with the Submission workflow.

docs.title: In this section
docs.text:
• Nowcast: the current nowcast of every model.
  • Backtest: every model scored on past releases.
  • Comparison with hub forecasts: our models against the hub teams.
  • Data: the hub data and how we read it.
  • Methods: the foundation models, the baseline models, evaluation and the pairing sensitivity.
  • Submission: the workflow, the hub specification, opting in and the submission log.

The code is in bdbvhub.

Next: Nowcast.

docs.title: Baseline models
docs.text:
The random walk nowcast and the random walk.

The random walk nowcast (randomwalknowcast) nowcasts the most recent weeks from the reporting delay of past releases, using our port of the baselinenowcast method, and forecasts each nowcast draw forward with a random walk on the log scale. The random walk (randomwalk) is the same walk started from the latest complete week, with no nowcast. Their methods, equations, differences between case studies and limitations are in the paper's supporting information.

The code is in nowcastbaselines, and which module does what is on the Implementation page. How their province draws are paired is under Correlated trajectories. The data and notation are on the Data methods page.

docs.title: Data
docs.text:
Extraction of the hub data, its vintages, and the synthetic vintages used in testing.

What the data show is on the Data results page.

docs.title: Target and notation
docs.text: The target is \(y_{p}(w)\), the final count of confirmed cases in province \(p\) with symptom onset in epi week \(w\) (Sunday to Saturday, labelled by its Saturday). It includes onsets the hub imputes for cases reported without one. A vintage \(v\) is the data of one hub release. It gives, for each \(p\) and \(w\), known onsets, imputed onsets and their total \(Y_{p,v}(w)\). A forecast made from vintage \(v\) serves the round with reference date \(r_v\), the first Saturday whose submission window (Sunday to Tuesday, Kinshasa time) closes on or after the vintage date. Horizon \(h\) is the number of weeks from \(r_v\) to \(w\). Backtest forecasts cover \(h = -4, \dots, 3\).

docs.title: Extraction
docs.text:
Hub file What it holds Vintages target-data/time-series.csv Weekly confirmed cases by onset week, by province and nationally. Also health zone totals. All, in one file auxiliary-data/daily-confirmed-case.csv Daily cases by onset day, observed and imputed, nationally and by province and health zone. The observed and imputed split of the weekly target comes from here. All, in one file auxiliary-data/weekly-reporting-delays-by-province.csv One row per known-onset case: province, onset week and onset-to-report delay. Latest only; earlier ones from the archive folder and git history auxiliary-data/locations.csv Location codes, names, types and parents. Static auxiliary-data/health-zone-code-mapping.csv Health zone codes mapped to P-codes and DHIS2 codes. Static hub-config/*.json Rounds, tasks, output types, hub settings and the metadata schema. Copied at download

The hub does not publish deaths, suspected cases, counts by report date or populations. Province populations are the Institut National de la Statistique's 2019 figures (Annuaire statistique RDC 2020), and province centres the means of health zone centroids weighted by WorldPop 2025 counts, as in BVDOutbreakSize.

docs.title: Vintages
docs.text: Each hub release is a vintage, labelled by its as_of date and of kind real or simulated. From the 2026-11-01 release on, as_of is the extraction date, a day after the last reported case. The hub states that earlier releases were labelled by the last reported case (hub issue 90). We keep each release's published label and map a rewritten label back to it. The data cut-off of a real release is its latest onset day over all places, one date per release. This gives 2026-10-07 for the release labelled 2026-10-09, 2026-10-16 for 2026-10-17 and 2026-10-31 for 2026-11-01. The last day or two before extraction are thin, as new reports take time to reach the line list. The latest onset day is a cut-off taken from the data that every model can share. The renewal models learn the publication lag from consecutive releases relative to this cut-off, so the lag adjusts to it and is not counted twice. A simulated release states its cut-off. The models, the scoring and the zone stage all use this cut-off. Recent weeks are revised in later releases, so each forecast is made from one vintage and scored on the counts later releases report.

docs.title: Release snapshots
docs.text: auxiliary-data/daily-confirmed-case.csv holds, for each release, the daily onsets known at that release. The count of a day is its known plus imputed onsets, and the counts of a week sum to the hub's weekly target. A release has an as_of date and a data cut-off (Vintages). A release observes the days up to its cut-off, and a day in range with no row counts 0. The baseline models compare the counts of a day across releases by its age at each cut-off (supporting information).

docs.title: Delay and missingness data
docs.text: The hub imputes an onset for each case reported without one by subtracting a delay drawn from a fit to its published delays (hub issue 61, supporting information). So the share of cases without an onset is measured at every vintage.

docs.title: BVDOutbreakSize estimates
docs.text: renewalbvd uses the Rt estimates in the public results-<run> releases of BVDOutbreakSize (MIT licence, Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.20312758). These are the national \(R_T\) draws, the patch summaries with the national \(R_T\) they are relative to where the release has them, and the release's data cut-off. Which release a forecast uses, how growth rates are turned into \(R_T\) and how the estimates enter the model are in the paper's supporting information. The release's joint-fit R-hat is read from the fit diagnostics table in its rendered site, and a release without a readable table is passed over for the next older one. Each fit records the release it used, its R-hat and why newer releases were skipped.

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text: Scoring, and the evaluations.

docs.title: What is scored
docs.text: Forecasts from real releases are scored on the count each later release reports, and on each week's count once its reporting is close to complete (Real releases).

docs.title: Scores
docs.text:
The hub takes sample trajectories, so every BDBV forecast is scored on its samples by the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS), as the paper scores Ebola. We use the fair form, scoringrules' crps_ensemble with estimator="fair", as defined in the paper's supporting information. CRPS on the log scale is the CRPS of the transformed target, \(\text{CRPS}(\log(1 + X), \log(1 + y))\), never the log of CRPS. CRPS on the natural scale is dominated by the places with the most cases. On the log scale it approximates a score of the relative error, close to a score of the growth rate, so every place counts on a similar footing2. CRPS, log CRPS and the energy score use the fair estimators for every model, ours and the hub teams'. Their expectation does not depend on the number of draws \(m\). So scores compare fairly although the number of draws differs across models and pages.

Forecasts Draws per forecast Set by Models the site runs itself in the release backtest and leave-one-province-out 1,000 [samples] backtest in packages/nowcastbdbv/config/backtest.toml Stored fits, the random walks' zone runs, the submission, the Nowcast page and our models in the Comparison with the hub 100 [forecast] n_samples in packages/nowcastbdbv/config/backtest.toml Hub teams 100 Their submissions German nowcast benchmark Quantiles at seven levels, scored by WIS packages/nowcastgermany/config/germany.toml

Every model shares the backtest's seed, so its draws use common random numbers. Each page states the counts it scores.

\[ \text{Bias} = 1 - \big(P(X \le y) + P(X \le y - 1)\big), \qquad \text{rCRPS}_m = \frac{\overline{\text{CRPS}}_m}{\overline{\text{CRPS}}_b}. \]

Positive bias is overprediction. Relative CRPS is a ratio of means against a baseline \(b\) over the forecasts both made, and below 1 beats it. Relative CRPS on the log scale is the same ratio of mean CRPS on the log scale. The baseline is randomwalknowcast, set by [scores] baseline in docs/site.toml. Of the Chronos-2 models the site shows only foundation ([models] in docs/site.toml); the others are still fitted, scored and in the paper. The interactive summaries and the checks chart have a Relative to picker that makes any model the baseline, and the overall score tables a baseline filter. In the summaries a new baseline changes which forecasts are matched, so \(n\) and the means change too. A model with every one of the baseline's forecasts has the baseline's \(n\), so those rows are read side by side. A model with fewer is marked partial, with its \(n\) of the baseline's, and comes after them, as its scores are on fewer forecasts. Coverage is whether \(y\) falls in the central 50% and 90% sample intervals.

docs.title: Energy score
docs.text:
The energy score scores one forecast of a vector \(\mathbf{y}\). For an origin, a release and a scale, \(\mathbf{y}\) holds every place at that scale in every scored week, and national holds the weeks only. It uses only the place-week cells that every compared model forecasts. Sample \(i\) of a model is its draws with sample index \(i\), \(\mathbf{X}_i\). We use the fair form over \(m\) samples, scoringrules' es_ensemble with estimator="fair", for every model (supporting information).

The energy score on the log scale is the energy score of \(\log(1 + \mathbf{y})\) against \(\log(1 + \mathbf{X}_i)\), never the log of the score. Relative energy scores are ratios of means against randomwalknowcast over the origins and releases both have, and \(n\) counts those. The score rewards a joint pattern across places only where draws are joint. The draws of renewal and renewalbvd are joint across zones and provinces, one posterior draw per sample index. renewalsp fits each zone on its own, so its zones are independent and its provinces are their sums. randomwalk and randomwalknowcast pair their province draws within each week by a rolling copula inside their forecast; their zones are not paired (Correlated trajectories). Hub teams' samples are joint across weeks within a place only, as the hub's sample format sets, so pairing their indices across places scores them as independent across places.

docs.title: Backtest design
docs.text:
Each vintage is a forecast task. The fitted models (the renewal models) forecast real vintages only, from their stored fits (fit store). The other models forecast every task.

Run Vintages Truth Development backtest Real, except the latest real vintage As for real releases Real releases Every real release with a later release The count each later release shows, and each week's count in the first release cut off the truth delay after it Comparison with hub forecasts Real where one serves the round The count each later release shows, and the latest release's count for its complete weeks

In leave-one-province-out, a week is complete when it ended at least 3 weeks before the truth vintage.

docs.title: Real releases
docs.text:
Each real release with a later release is an origin from the first release with at least two usable releases up to it (nowcasteval.backtest.backtest_origins). A cumulative first release (Data) is not usable, so the first origin is 2026-10-17. That first release, 2026-08-18, has no delay file. It is also 50 days before the next release, and its weeks three or more weeks old hold 88% to 97% of the counts the 2026-11-08 release gives them, against 93% to 102% in the releases between. It stays in the data of later origins. The random walk models forecast from the releases up to the origin only. The renewal models' stored forecasts from the origin are scored with them. So are hub teams' forecasts for a round, at the latest release serving it. A model that cannot forecast from an origin is listed with no forecasts there. Two targets are scored.

Reported. The count each later release \(o'\) shows for every forecast week it reports. randomwalk is scored on its samples as they are, with no delay. Every other model with a modelled delay forecasts the final count \(X\) of week \(w\), which is mapped to what \(o'\) shows by that delay.

  1. Day \(t\) is \(a = c - t\) days old at a cut-off \(c\), and \(\pi(a)\) is the share of its final count the model expects reported by then. For randomwalknowcast, \(\pi(a) = 1 / \Gamma(a)\) under the daily delay it fits at the origin (supporting information). For the renewal models it is the posterior median of each province's cumulative onset-to-report delay of the latest onset week, as the fit stores it. Ages past the end of the delay take its last value, and days after the cut-off have \(\pi = 0\).
  2. A week's share \(\pi_w\) is the mean of \(\pi\) over its seven days.
  3. Each place is mapped by the model's delay at that place, a zone with none by its province's, and a place with neither is scored as forecast. The renewal models' shared delay is the unweighted centre of the province delays, not a national delay, so the country is the sum of the mapped provinces.

  4. With \(R_o\) the count reported at the origin, the count outstanding there, \(X - R_o\), is thinned binomially, so each sample becomes a draw of the count reported at \(o'\),

    \[ R_o + \text{Binomial}(X - R_o, q), \qquad q = \frac{\pi_w(c_{o'}) - \pi_w(c_o)}{1 - \pi_w(c_o)}, \]

with the sign carried when \(X < R_o\), \(q\) kept in \([0, 1]\), and \(q = 1\) for a week fully reported at the origin. A model with no modelled delay, such as a hub team or a Chronos-2 model (Foundation models), is scored on complete weeks only.

Complete weeks. Each week's count in the first release whose cut-off is at least the truth delay after the week ends. The truth delay is truth_delay in packages/nowcastbdbv/config/backtest.toml. By default it is the age by which 98% of the national count is reported (truth_level). Each earlier release's national count of a week is set against the latest release's, at the week's age in that release rounded up to whole weeks, and the counts are pooled over releases at each age. The first age whose pooled share reaches 98% is the truth delay. The 2026-08-18 release is left out, as its old weeks were revised rather than late. Weeks with no release that far after them are not scored yet. The Backtest page gives the truth delay in use and how many forecasts it scores. Health zones are scored on the weeks the latest release reports in full. There a week is complete when it is at least 4 weeks back from the week holding the latest release's cut-off and grew by less than 2% since the release before.

Scores are CRPS, CRPS on the log scale, 50% and 90% coverage and bias, by model, origin, weeks back from the week holding the origin's cut-off, and place. Relative CRPS is against randomwalknowcast on the forecasts both made, for national and the provinces pooled, over all origins and by origin, and by origin and place. Every table counts its forecasts, \(n\), so a model with fewer forecasts was scored on fewer weeks or places. The run stops if an origin has no release snapshots or two models run here give identical samples.

docs.title: Correlated trajectories
docs.text:
randomwalk and randomwalknowcast draw each province on its own, so the country, the sum of the provinces, would be too narrow. Each pairs its province draws within each week by a Gaussian copula, with a correlation estimated from its own matured errors. The copula, its estimator and how its settings were chosen are in the paper's supporting information.

The pairing is inside each model's own forecast (nowcastbaselines.copula.pair_walks), so the fit store, every page, the backtests and the submissions read the same paired draws. The renewal models' draws are already joint trajectories, so they are left as they are: reordering would break their real dependence. renewal and renewalbvd fit their zones jointly and sum them to provinces, and renewalsp fits each zone on its own and sums them to provinces. Each forecast's \(\rho_p\), the pairs behind it and whether it fell back to the prior are recorded (a submission's copula.json). How much pairing matters is on the Pairing sensitivity page.

docs.title: Reading the figures
docs.text: Fans show 100 sample trajectories, the 50% and 90% bands and the median. In point-and-line figures, points are medians, thick lines 50% intervals and thin lines 90% intervals. The data at the origin are dashed, shown when the origin is not the latest vintage, and the data as later reported are solid. The dotted vertical line is the reference date. Weeks still being reported are shaded, with hollow points. The vertical axis of a fan ends at the top of its 90% band. Horizon is weeks from the reference week, so negative horizons are nowcasts, 0 is the reference week and positive horizons are forecasts.

docs.title: Leave-one-province-out
docs.text: One province's counts are left out of the likelihood while it stays in the model (supporting information). This removes the known and imputed counts of its zones and its delay counts but keeps its zones in the latent process. In renewalbvd it also drops the national BVDOutbreakSize term and the patch that holds the province. renewalsp fits each zone only on its own data, so it cannot forecast a province left out. Its onsets are scored against the latest real vintage on the complete weeks. It runs on every real vintage for the three renewal models.

docs.title: Health zones
docs.text: randomwalk and randomwalknowcast are scored at zone level, for every zone with cases at the vintage (supporting information). A week with no onsets in a zone has a count of 0. Each model's zone samples are its zone run at the origin, which the fit store holds for every hub zone, scored as the model draws them, as in the submitted file. Each real vintage before the latest is forecast, and origins with only one release are skipped, as for provinces. Zones are scored on the reported target as for real releases, with the zone delays fitted at the origin, so a zone count is never scored against a count still being reported. Relative CRPS is against randomwalknowcast. On the Nowcast page every model is shown at zone level: the random walks from their stored zone runs, and the fitted models from the zone samples of their stored forecasts (Renewal models). The Comparison with the hub scores every model's zone samples on the zone cells the hub teams forecast.

docs.title: Scores by place type and plausibility
docs.text: The scores on the reported target, at province and zone level, are also averaged by the type of place and by a plausibility flag of each forecast, both decided from the counts reported at the origin. Relative CRPS in these averages is against randomwalknowcast. Week \(w\) is the latest week ending on or before the origin, and \(n(t)\) the count reported then for the week ending \(t\), with 0 for a week with no row. A place with no case in the 9 weeks to \(w\), one with no week above 5 cases, and the rest form the three place types. The flag is set from each origin's forecast of week \(w + 1\), with median \(q_{50}\) and 95% quantile \(q_{95}\). This is the round's reference week for an origin from Saturday to Tuesday, and the week before it for an origin from Wednesday to Friday. The level is \(L = \max\{(n(w - 3) + n(w - 2)) / 2,\ n(w - 1)\}\) and the recent maximum is \(M = \max(1, \max_{w - 4 \le t \le w} n(t))\). A forecast collapses if \(L \ge 3\) and \(q_{50} \le L / 3\). Otherwise it blows up if \(q_{50} > 3M\) and \(q_{50} - M \ge 5\), or \(q_{95} > 10M\) and \(q_{95} - M \ge 20\). A forecast with neither has no flag. Every scored week of a forecast takes the forecast's place type and flag, and the scores are averaged over scored weeks.

docs.title: Comparison with hub forecasts
docs.text: For each hub reference date, our unfitted models forecast from the latest real vintage serving the round. Fitted models use their stored fits for the same round, every week the fit forecast. Where we submitted to a round, our submitted file is a series of its own beside these main-build forecasts. Every model is scored only on the hub teams' cells: the rounds, places and weeks any team forecast. Our models forecast more places and weeks, and rounds no team forecast, and those cells are not scored. Each cell is scored on the complete weeks, from the vintage serving the round, since hub teams have no modelled delay we can see. The table by round gives each model's n beside hub_cells, the team cells scored, so a model with fewer missed some. CRPS is relative to randomwalknowcast on the weeks both forecast, on the comparison page. A round is pending until a later real release exists.

docs.title: German nowcast benchmark
docs.text:
The German COVID-19 hospitalisation nowcasting hub1 collected nowcasts of the 7-day hospitalisation incidence by Meldedatum, the date a case was reported positive, for Germany, its 16 states and six age groups. randomwalk and randomwalknowcast run on its data unchanged, as follows.

  1. Each day's data version is a release whose cut-off is that day, and the Meldedatum is the onset date. A release's count of a day is the count reported by then in the hub's reporting triangle, with the changes after 80 days put at 81 days, as epinowcast's germany_covid19_hosp does. A day's last count is carried to every later release.
  2. Germany is the country. The states are its provinces in one task and Germany's age groups its provinces in another. Germany's nowcast is the sum of the states.
  3. The hub's targets are the 7-day sums ending on every day from the nowcast date to 28 days before it. Each nowcast date is forecast once, so every sum comes from one forecast with one context end. Models of daily steps read each day's 7-day sum from their own rolling-sum row (reporting-triangle layout) or sum their daily draws (complete layout). Dates are real: the nowcast date is the cut-off, whatever its weekday. Models of weekly steps forecast the sums that end on a Saturday.
  4. randomwalk and randomwalknowcast pair their draws inside their forecast, as on BDBV (Correlated trajectories). Each state's and age group's nowcast is unchanged, and Germany's, the sum of the paired states, widens.

The nowcast dates are the paper's, every day from 2021-11-22 to 2022-04-29. They are split at their midpoint. The 80 dates before 2022-02-10 are for developing and checking our setup. The 79 dates from 2022-02-10 on are held out for the paper and are not scored here. The hub collected nowcasts as quantiles at the levels 2.5%, 10%, 25%, 50%, 75%, 90% and 97.5%. Our models' samples are reduced to their quantiles at these levels, as for a hub submission. Our models and the hub teams are then scored the same way, as the paper did. The scores are the weighted interval score (WIS) of the seven quantiles, the absolute error of the median and the coverage of the 50% and 95% intervals. These are quantile forecasts, so this benchmark keeps WIS where the BDBV pages use CRPS. With quantiles \(q_\tau\) at the \(2K + 1\) levels \(\tau\),

$$ \text{WIS}(F, y) = \frac{1}{K + 1/2} \sum_{\tau} \left(\mathbb{1}{y < q_\tau} - \tau\right)\left(q_\tau - y\right), \qquad K = 3. $$ Each 7-day sum's truth is its count in the data 40 days after it ends, the paper's 40-day truth. Our models see only reports made within 40 days of each reference date, so they forecast the count the truth holds. The backtest scores its complete weeks the same way, on the first release the truth delay after each week (Real releases). Relative scores divide a model's mean score by randomwalknowcast's on the nowcasts both made. The paper's relative scores divide by the hub's own baseline, KIT-frozen_baseline. Both baselines are set in packages/nowcastgermany/config/germany.toml. nowcastgermany paper writes every forecast, with its truth, as the paper's long table.

The teams' nowcasts are those the paper gathered, prospective and retrospective, at the horizons our models give. Two fixes are the paper's. RKI's quantiles above one million are errors, replaced by its -1 day nowcast. Epiforecasts' missing 10% quantile is filled from the normal through its 2.5% and 25% quantiles. Under 1% of the teams' forecasts have quantiles that cross, and their values are sorted within the forecast. The paper also filled some missing ILM and LMU nowcasts from later model versions, and those are not scored here.

  1. Wolffram D, Abbott S, an der Heiden M, Funk S, Günther F, Hailer D, et al. (2023). Collaborative nowcasting of COVID-19 hospitalization incidences in Germany. PLOS Computational Biology 19(8): e1011394. doi:10.1371/journal.pcbi.1011394. ↩

  2. Bosse NI, Abbott S, Cori A, van Leeuwen E, Bracher J, Funk S (2023). Scoring epidemiological forecasts on transformed scales. PLOS Computational Biology 19(8): e1011393. doi:10.1371/journal.pcbi.1011393. ↩

docs.title: Using the fine-tuned model
docs.text:
How to nowcast your own reporting triangle with the Chronos-2 checkpoints we fine-tuned on simulated outbreaks.

Each fine-tuned checkpoint is a GitHub release of this repository, chronos-ft-<hash>, where the hash is that of the fine-tuning settings. A release holds a LoRA adapter for Chronos-2, the settings that made it (settings.json) and the SHA-256 of each file (sha256sums.txt). How the checkpoints are made is in the paper's supporting information. Fine-tuning runs locally, not on CI.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
uv add "nowcastfoundation @ git+https://github.com/seabbs/bdbv-hub-modelling#subdirectory=packages/nowcastfoundation"
uv add chronos-forecasting==2.3.2 "peft>=0.17" "torch>=2.7"

In a clone of this repository, uv sync --group chronos does the same. Chronos-2 runs on a CPU, a CUDA GPU or an Apple GPU. Set GH_TOKEN or GITHUB_TOKEN to a GitHub token if you list releases often, as anonymous requests are rate limited.

docs.title: Load a checkpoint
docs.text:
chronos_ft.load takes "latest", the newest chronos-ft-* release by publish date, or a settings hash, which pins that release. It downloads the adapter once to ~/.cache/bdbv-hub-modelling/chronos-ft-<hash>. It checks each adapter file against the release's sha256sums.txt, on download and on every later use, and fails if one differs. The check catches a damaged download, not a release whose files were replaced, as the sums come from the same release. Pin a hash for reproducible work, and record the SHA-256 in model.checkpoint.sha256 with your results. A process resolves "latest" once, so restart it to pick up a newer release.

from nowcastfoundation import checkpoints as chronos_ft

model = chronos_ft.load("e8a1f5ae338b")
model.checkpoint.hash, model.adapter

docs.title: Forecast a reporting triangle
docs.text:
chronos_ft.forecast_triangle takes a data frame with one row per reference time and one column per delay from 0. Each cell is the count first reported at that delay. The rows must be in increasing, equally spaced order, the columns the delays 0, 1, 2 and so on, and the last row's cut-off sets what is known: row \(t\) of \(T\) is reported up to delay \(T - 1 - t\). Cells after that are ignored, so they may be NaN. A missing cell before it is an error; give 0 where nothing was reported. The last delay is taken as final.

The rows reported at every delay are Chronos-2's context. Each count at each earlier delay is a covariate, known up to the last cut-off. This is the reporting-triangle layout of the foundation model (Layouts). Our checkpoints were fine-tuned with last delays of 2 to 7 weeks or 14 to 49 days, so triangles in those ranges match their training best.

The output has one row per place, reference time and quantile level:

Column Meaning place series, or the key of each triangle when given a dict of places reference the row's reference time, extended past the last row for dates and numbers step rows after the last: 0 is the last row, below 0 the rows still being reported, above 0 rows ahead (horizon) quantile_level the level, Chronos-2's own unless quantile_levels is given value the quantile of the row's final count

A dict of triangles, one per place with the same rows and delays, is forecast as one group, so Chronos-2 sees every place at once. model=None uses the pretrained Chronos-2, for a comparison with the fine-tuned one.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
--8 < --"chronos_ft.py"

The test suite runs this example with a stand-in for Chronos-2 (packages/nowcastfoundation/tests/test_chronos_ft.py).

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• The checkpoints were fine-tuned on simulated Ebola-like outbreaks for the BDBV hub. Check them on your own data before relying on them.
  • Quantiles are Chronos-2's for each row on its own. They are not joint draws, so they do not give the distribution of sums over rows.
  • "latest" changes when a new release is published. Record model.checkpoint.hash with your results.

docs.title: Foundation models
docs.text:
The foundation model and its comparison variants give the hub target's releases to the Chronos-2 time series foundation model1.

The data and notation are on the Data methods page. foundation is Chronos-2 fine-tuned on simulated outbreaks (Fine-tuning) on the reporting-triangle layout. The variants the paper compares it with are foundation_zeroshot (pretrained weights), foundation_zeroshot_complete and foundation_complete (complete layout), foundation_baselinenowcast and foundation_zeroshot_baselinenowcast (baselinenowcast), and foundation_real (fine-tuned on real data alone). None is fitted to these data: Chronos-2 forecasts in context, from its pretrained weights or a fine-tuned checkpoint. Only foundation runs in the Fit store and the submission; the variants are run by the paper's workflow alone. Each model reads the cadence from the data: one pass on the daily releases gives the daily counts and the weekly hub target, and a task with weekly releases only gives the weekly target. The hub model seabbs-foundation is set up to submit foundation and is off until it is opted in (Opting in).

In brief, each model:

  1. lays out the hub target of every release by place, step and release lag (Releases);
  2. puts every hub target, the country, the provinces and their health zones, each as its own series, in one block that Chronos-2 forecasts jointly (Layouts);
  3. draws 100 trajectories from Chronos-2's quantiles (Trajectories);
  4. rounds the draws to counts (Counts).

docs.title: Releases
docs.text:
The target is the hub's: confirmed cases by onset week, known and imputed onsets together. Two sources give it with its updates; a model takes the daily one when the task has daily releases.

  • Daily: the daily counts of each release, known plus imputed onsets. A step is an onset day.
  • Weekly: the weekly counts of each release of the target data, for the country, the provinces and the zones. A step is an onset week.

For place \(p\), step \(t\) and release \(r\) with cut-off in step \(c_r\), the release lag is \(d = c_r - t\). \(Y_{p,t,d}\) is the count of step \(t\) at lag \(d\), from the release whose cut-off is \(d\) steps after \(t\). Release \(r\) gives lag \(d\) only at step \(c_r - d\), so each lag has at most one value per release and is missing at other steps. \(X_{p,t}\) is the count of step \(t\) at the vintage, with cut-off step \(c\).

docs.title: Layouts
docs.text:
Every hub target is a series in one block: the country, all 26 provinces, and every health zone of those provinces. Each is the hub target itself, so the country is not the sum of the provinces and the zones are not split from them. Zone counts are zero before the zone releases start. Chronos-2 forecasts every target series in the block jointly, from one shared last step of context, \(t^*\), which each layout sets differently.

  • Complete (*_complete): the targets \(X_{p,t}\) for \(t \le t^*\). \(t^*\) is the earliest over places of the week randomwalk starts its walk from, the latest week 95% complete under its delay (supporting information). It comes from the delay alone, so it needs no walk spread.
  • Reporting triangle (*_ragged): the same targets, with one lag series per place with cases and lag \(d < D\), indexed by onset step as in a regression nowcast. Lag series \(d\) holds \(Y_{p,t,d}\), missing where it is not yet reported, and Chronos-2 masks the missing values. \(t^* = c - D\), the last step whose count is at lag \(D\) or more, with \(D\) estimated from the data (lag_count). \(D\) is the first lag at which the steps 28 to 112 days (4 to 16 weeks) before the cut-off had 99% of their counts reported, pooled over places and releases, read from no release after the cut-off. It is at most 112 days or 16 weeks and at most what the history allows, with two steps of context before the longest lag, and that many when the window has no counts or never reaches 99%. A model can fix \(D\) instead (lags); the SI compares the estimate with 4 weeks or 28 days. The lag series run past \(t^*\) as known future values, which is how recent counts reach the nowcast. A place with no cases has no lag series, as they would be all zero. The daily block also has each place's 7-day rolling sum as a series (rolling7), so the hub's 7-day target is a series of the block. So the daily block, where 75 of 546 places have cases, fits in memory.

Chronos-2 standardises each series and takes its arcsinh, so counts go in as they are.

docs.title: Trajectories
docs.text: Chronos-2 gives 21 quantiles, from 1% to 99%, of each series at each step ahead. Each of the 100 trajectories reads each series and step's quantile function at a uniform level: linear between the quantiles and flat beyond them. The levels are coupled at each forecast by one step, nowcastutils.trajectories.choose_coupling, which chooses the coupling from the data. Its candidates are a Gaussian copula (couple), with correlation rho between consecutive steps of a series and s between series, fitted (fit_coupling) over the earlier releases of the latest 14, 28 or 56 days, the Schaake shuffle, each sample ordered as one past window of the series' own reported values (history_windows), and comonotone draws (one level per sample and series). The earlier releases are every release in the 70 days before the task's (coupling_releases), and the model forecasts the same block at each. Each of those forecasts is scored at the steps that are final by the task's release, as normal scores of its randomised PIT (pit_scores), which the Gaussian fit reads. Each release with at least two before it is a test: every candidate is fitted from what came before it, its draws are scored against what has been reported since (energy score), and the candidate with the lowest mean score is fitted from everything before the task and used. A candidate that cannot be fitted at one of the tests (the Schaake shuffle with too little history) drops out. With nothing to compare on, the Gaussian over the longest window is used when there are two releases to fit it from, else the Schaake shuffle, else independence. On the German development half the step's draws give sums over the nowcast days 9 to 15% lower CRPS than independent draws (nowcasteval.coupling). The chosen coupling, its fit and each candidate's score are written beside a submission (copula.json). The candidate windows are the only settings; which is used is chosen at each forecast. Independent and comonotone draws remain as named options (coupling) for the supplement.

docs.title: Counts
docs.text: A draw is rounded to the nearest count and floored at zero. Steps up to \(t^*\) are their count at the vintage. The hub's target is weekly. A daily reporting-triangle model reads each week from its place's rolling 7-day series on the week's last day, and a daily complete model sums its seven daily draws.

docs.title: Patches and context
docs.text: Chronos-2 reads a series in patches of 16 steps. The context is every step from the first onset in the releases to \(t^*\).

docs.title: Scoring
docs.text: The models forecast final counts and model no delay. So the release backtest scores them on the complete target only, each week against the first release the truth delay after it ends (Evaluation).

docs.title: Health zones
docs.text: The models forecast the zones themselves, as series of the block. The country, provinces and zones all come straight from the block, daily or weekly as the model runs. Nothing is summed or split, so zones need not sum to their province. Each zone keeps its published count, as every series does. So the stored forecasts, the hub file and the scores all have the zones as submitted. The renewal models fit the zones and sum them to their provinces instead (Health zones).

docs.title: Fine-tuning
docs.text:
The fine-tuned models (foundation, foundation_complete, foundation_baselinenowcast) load one LoRA checkpoint of Chronos-2, fine-tuned on simulated outbreaks whose reporting follows epinowcast's observation model. The simulations, the training and the checkpoints' scores are in the paper's supporting information, and how to load a checkpoint is on Using the fine-tuned model. The simulator is nowcastfoundation.simulator (the design and value draws, then each simulation as the joint PyRenew model in nowcastrenewal.simulation.outbreak), run on the grid config packages/nowcastfoundation/config/finetune/grid.yaml by the workflow's simulate_batch rule; the training blocks are cut by nowcastfoundation.finetune.training_block, and the block design and release cadences are BLOCK_DESIGN in nowcastfoundation.finetune.chronos and finetune.release_days; the workflow README says which rounds a run trains on.

A checkpoint is named by its settings hash, of the blocks, the code and the training settings. The first release, chronos-ft-2c2b22a03107, was trained from earlier code, so its hash cannot be reproduced from this repository. Later releases are trained from the code here, so retraining from it gives the same hash. Each checkpoint is published as the repository's release chronos-slots-<hash> (with the series bias) or chronos-ft-<hash>, with a sha256sums.txt of its files. The models load the newest such release by publish date (hash = "latest" in packages/nowcastfoundation/config/finetune.toml), so each new release, interim or final, is picked up; a settings hash there pins one release instead. source in packages/nowcastfoundation/config/finetune.toml says where the checkpoint is read from: github (the release), huggingface (a Hugging Face Hub repository at a pinned revision holding the same files) or local (a training segment folder). A checkpoint read from the Hub is the same checkpoint as its release, so it keys the same stored fits. The checkpoint's hash and adapter SHA-256 key the stored fits, so a new release refits the fine-tuned models, and each stored fit records the checkpoint it used. The adapter is downloaded once and checked against sha256sums.txt and the settings hash. The fit store resolves the release once per run, with the workflow's GitHub token, and passes its hash to every fit in BDBV_CHRONOS_FT. If GitHub cannot be reached, building a model fails rather than fall back to a checkpoint downloaded before. A fit whose adapter cannot be downloaded is stored as failed, and the fit store keeps it until its inputs change. Such fits are retried by running the Fit store workflow with retry_failed (gh workflow run fit-store.yml -R seabbs/bdbv-hub-modelling -f retry_failed=true -f models="foundation foundation").

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• The zero-shot models use Chronos-2 as pretrained. It has not seen these data or outbreaks like them.
  • The fine-tuned models have seen only simulated outbreaks, whose delays and dynamics may not match these data.
  • The fine-tuned models were trained on blocks no larger than the memory budget allows, but forecast all 546 hub targets in one block.
  • Draws are independent across steps and places, so a weekly value of the daily complete model, a sum of seven daily draws, is too narrow, as are sums over weeks or places.

  1. Ansari A F et al. (2025) Chronos-2: From univariate to universal forecasting. arXiv:2510.15821. Code: https://github.com/amazon-science/chronos-forecasting. ↩

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text: How the models are built in code, computed and sampled.

docs.title: Code
docs.text: The model extends PyRenew, pinned to a commit, and runs in JAX with NumPyro. Its code is in nowcastrenewal.model and the variants are in nowcastrenewal.forecaster. The model is configured by ModelConfig.

docs.title: PyRenew and what is built here
docs.text:
Component PyRenew piece Built here Pooled \(R_p(t)\) BaseSubpopulationInfections, WeeklyTemporalProcess NonCentredRandomWalk, for the frozen seeding weeks, the separate forecast steps and their reversion. Renewal with importation and depletion BaseSubpopulationInfections, subclassed the shared components.renewal.run_renewal, called from _infections_from_rt, and the shared components.mixing.Mixing, which gives the mixing matrix as PyRenew's mobility_matrix_rv does. Ascertainment \(\alpha(s)\) IndependentAscertainment with a temporal process None. Onset-to-report delay \(f_{p,s}(d)\) None HazardDelay, with province offsets and drifts from pooled_walk, as the Rt deviations. Missing onsets \(m_p(t)\) None MissingOnsetFraction, a pooled walk of the same form as \(R_p\) with its own parameters. Known and imputed onsets BaseObservationProcess with temporal_pmf_rv for the infection-to-onset pmf (the incubation period, a CensoredPMF with a random mean and SD), NegativeBinomialNoise, compute_prop_already_reported for the publication lag OnsetStreams. Publication lag None A Dirichlet simplex fitted to consecutive releases by ReleasePairLikelihood. Delays of known-onset cases None DirichletMultinomialNoise, a noise model in the form of PyRenew's CountNoise for counts by delay given weekly totals. BVDOutbreakSize Rt None RtPseudoObservation, a RandomVariable the latent process calls, as it holds both \(R\) and infections.

PyRenew pieces that give a different model, sample less well, or would only rename one line, are not used.

  • The RandomWalk temporal process puts the step SD in the step distribution, so it is centred in the SD.
  • ARProcess gives the same walk, log density and gradient, but NUTS needs more tree steps with it, so the walk samples its steps as one vectorised site.
  • AR1 draws its first state from the stationary distribution, and DifferencedAR1 is AR(1) on the differences. Here walks start at a fixed value and stay there over the seeding weeks.
  • SubpopulationInfections samples one deviation process per province and subtracts their mean, which leaves a direction the data do not identify. Here the \(P_s - 1\) coordinates on the sum-to-zero basis \(Q\) of the seeded provinces are sampled.
  • HierarchicalNormalPrior has no sum-to-zero constraint. On the basis coordinates it is the same prior, but it would replace one sample statement.
  • GammaGroupSdPrior gives each province its own SD with a floor, where here the provinces share one half-normal SD.
  • CountObservation and SubpopulationCounts take one fixed delay pmf and one truncation pmf. Here the delay varies with onset day, and known and imputed onsets are separate streams.
  • MobilitySubpopulationInfections uses a fixed mobility matrix, \(R\) by location and depletion capped at the susceptibles. Here a share of transmission is sent from each origin through a fixed gravity kernel, and depletion is exponential in the pool \(\nu\).

PyRenew has no delay that varies with time, no Dirichlet-multinomial count and no pseudo-observation of \(R\).

docs.title: Baseline models
docs.text:
The baselines are in nowcastbaselines.randomwalk on a JAX port of baselinenowcast 0.2.2 in nowcastbaselines.baselinenowcast. The port is checked live against the R package. Its chain ladder also takes its factors from pairs of consecutive release snapshots, skipping the cells a release does not observe, and fits one daily delay shared by pairs of any gap. On daily releases this is the R package's chain ladder. The models use it in baselinenowcast.nowcast, with the delay in baselinenowcast.delays and the observation model in baselinenowcast.uncertainty, which fits and draws new reports with the port's fit_by_horizon, fit_nb and sample_nb.

Part Where Snapshots as arrays [location, release, day] nowcastutils.snapshots Pair sums, the daily delay fit and growth baselinenowcast.delays, pair sums jit with locations on the leading axis Own or pooled source of each estimate nowcastbaselines.pooling New reports on the count to come baselinenowcast.uncertainty One random walk for both models nowcastbaselines.walk Introductions into places with no recent case nowcastbaselines.introductions Zone samples that sum to the province samples nowcastbaselines.zones Backtest on real releases nowcasteval.nowcast

Shapes are fixed within an origin, so each new origin compiles once. Pandas only builds the inputs and the output frames.

docs.title: Numerics
docs.text:
The model runs in single precision (float32), JAX's default.

  • Depletion is carried on \(\log S\), which needs no subtraction, and \(1 - e^{-y}\) is computed with expm1.
  • The generation interval, the incubation period and the hub's imputation delay are double interval censored in closed form, \(G(d + 1) - 2G(d) + G(d - 1)\) with the integrated cdf (components.pmfs, primarycensored's form). The generation interval is computed once and the hub's delay once per release, both in float64, and the incubation period in float32 at each draw of its mean and SD (CensoredPMF); all match primarycensored.
  • The simulator's delays use the same closed form, truncated at their maximum delay and renormalised as primarycensored's \(D\). In float64 they are within \(10^{-8}\) of primarycensored, and in float32 within \(4 \times 10^{-5}\) of numerical integration.
  • The negative binomial size is kept below 1000, which is Poisson for these counts, and the Dirichlet-multinomial concentration below \(10^4\) (supporting information).
  • The hub imputation sums are products of banded \(7 \times 7k\) blocks for each onset week, so the cost grows with the number of weeks and not its square.

The tests check the renewal and the imputation against a NumPy reference, tests/model/numpy_reference.py.

docs.title: Sampling
docs.text:
PyRenew's PyrenewBuilder builds each model as a MultiSignalModel, and NumPyro's NUTS fits it. Chains run vectorised unless a fit's settings say otherwise. Stored fits run their chains in parallel. Without other settings, NUTS runs 4 chains of 1000 warm-up and 1000 draws, with target acceptance 0.9 and maximum tree depth 10. Each chain starts from its own draw from the prior. The fit store's fits, which the backtest and the submission read, take each model's settings from its candidate in packages/bdbvsubmission/policy.toml. Those settings, and the convergence checks that rule a fit out, are in the paper's supporting information. Leave-one-province-out fits take theirs from [sampler] in packages/nowcastbdbv/config/backtest.toml when BDBV_RENEWAL_SAMPLER is unset. Each fit reports its largest R-hat over parameters and the share of draws at the maximum tree depth.

The parameterisation is as follows.

  • Every walk, the pooled \(\log R(t)\) included, samples its steps non-centred, as standard normals scaled by the step SD.
  • Province deviations sum to zero through an orthonormal basis \(Q\) of the sum-to-zero subspace of the seeded provinces, so the \(P_s - 1\) free processes are unconstrained.
  • The starting offsets of the \(\log R\) deviations are sampled centred, and those of the missing-onset fraction non-centred.
  • Walk steps after the fit axis are not sampled by NUTS. They are drawn from the prior given each posterior draw when forecasting.

docs.title: Renewal models
docs.text:
The three renewal models, and what their fits give the site and the hub.

renewal fits the health zones with recent cases together, nests them in their provinces, pools them and links them by importation. renewalbvd is renewal with a down-weighted likelihood term on the Rt of BVDOutbreakSize. renewalsp fits the same model to each health zone on its own, with no pooling or importation. Their methods, equations, priors and limitations are in the paper's supporting information. How the models are built in code and sampled is on the Implementation page.

The zone fits are in zones.py and model/zones.py. seabbs-renewal submits the first of renewalbvd, renewalsp, renewal, randomwalknowcast and randomwalk, in that order, to pass its checks (Submission workflow). A release with national cases in no province stops the fit (check_national), since no release has had any (data/national-coherence.csv).

flowchart TD
    PM["<b>Place model</b><br/>Rt walk<br/>generation interval<br/>onsets and delay<br/>missing onsets<br/>three data streams"]
    RN["<b>renewal</b><br/>zones with recent cases<br/>fitted together<br/>+ pooled log R walk<br/>+ province and zone<br/>sum-to-zero AR(1) deviations<br/>+ importation between zones<br/>+ share at risk<br/>+ delay pooled by province<br/>+ silent zones by the<br/>fitted importation<br/>provinces are zone sums"]
    BV["<b>renewalbvd</b><br/>+ BVDOutbreakSize Rt,<br/>SDs inflated (κ = 1.5)"]
    SP["<b>renewalsp</b><br/>each zone fitted alone<br/>no pooling or importation<br/>+ share at risk"]

    PM -- "nest zones in provinces" --> RN
    RN -- "add external Rt" --> BV
    PM -- "fit each zone alone" --> SP

docs.title: Weekly Rt
docs.text: Each fit also gives the hub's wk R_t target, the weekly effective reproduction number by week of infection. For place \(p\) and week \(w\) it is the daily effective Rt (Rt times the susceptible share) weighted by that day's infections, $\(R_{p,w} = \frac{\sum_{t \in w} I_p(t) R^{\text{eff}}_p(t)}{\sum_{t \in w} I_p(t)}.\)$ A province above fitted zones and the country pool their fitted places in the same way, weighting each by \(\sum_{t \in w} I_p(t)\), draw by draw. Rt is given for the fitted zones, the provinces above them and the country. A zone is fitted if it had a case in the 9 weeks to the cut-off, the random walks' walk window (Baseline models). Places outside the fit have no Rt and add nothing to their province or the country. We submit every location in rt.csv.gz, for the week before the reference date and the reference week. Fits of zones on their own (renewalsp) pair draws by index, as their trajectories do. The quantiles are taken over every posterior draw, not the 100 trajectories, and weeks after the data take the forecast Rt. The fit directory holds them as rt.csv.gz (location, target_end_date, output_type_id, value). This Rt is estimated from the hub's onsets, including its imputed onsets, so it is likely to react more slowly than transmission (hub issue 61).

docs.title: Health zones
docs.text: Zones do not enter the national value. renewal and renewalbvd forecast the zones themselves, and their provinces are the zone sums. randomwalk and randomwalknowcast forecast each zone from its own data (supporting information). The foundation models take their zones straight from their joint block, as their provinces and country, so their zones need not sum to the provinces either (Foundation models). renewalsp fits each zone on its own, and its provinces are the zone sums too. The stored fits, the scores, the site and the submission all read these zone samples.
